This paper tackles an important and underexplored problem: helping users manage privacy risks arising from voluntary online self-disclosure. The paper makes three main contributions: a span-level taxonomy and annotated corpus of self-disclosures on Reddit, a token/span tagging model for identifying disclosures, and a new generation task of “self-disclosure abstraction” that aims to rewrite disclosures into less specific forms while preserving utility. The topic is timely, societally meaningful, and well aligned with growing interest in user-facing privacy tools rather than only adversarial/privacy-leakage analyses. I found the paper ambitious and interesting, especially in its attempt to combine NLP modeling with a user study and a generation component.

The strongest aspect of the paper is the problem framing. Much prior work indeed focuses either on PII detection/redaction or on coarse sentence/post-level self-disclosure classification. The move to span-level identification is practically meaningful: if the goal is to support users in editing text before posting, highlighting exact spans is much more actionable than assigning a post-level label. The proposed taxonomy of 19 categories is also a useful step toward broader coverage than standard PII tools. The inclusion of an HCI study is another strength, because it grounds the work in actual user perceptions rather than benchmark metrics alone. Finally, the abstraction task is novel and intuitively compelling as a middle ground between full redaction and leaving text unchanged.

That said, while the paper is promising, I have substantial concerns about methodological rigor, evaluation design, and the strength of some claims. My overall assessment is positive but cautious: the paper opens an important direction, but several parts feel preliminary, and some conclusions are stronger than the evidence currently supports.

On the dataset side, the corpus appears valuable, but key annotation details are missing or underdeveloped. The paper states that 10K posts were sampled, two annotators filtered for whether posts contain personal disclosure, and 2,415 posts were retained for span annotation. However, the review would benefit from much more transparency about annotation quality. I did not see inter-annotator agreement statistics for either the initial filtering stage or the span/category labeling stage. Given that the paper itself later emphasizes divergence between annotators and end users regarding what counts as risky or worth highlighting, agreement is especially important here. Without agreement numbers, it is difficult to judge whether the task is well defined and whether the reported model performance is approaching human consistency or far below it. Similarly, the paper mentions adjudication only for the two most recent batches used as test data, but it is unclear whether training data were singly or doubly annotated, how disagreements were resolved, and whether category definitions were stable over time. Since the taxonomy is central to the contribution, more evidence of annotation reliability is necessary.

Relatedly, the taxonomy itself is useful but somewhat conceptually uneven. Some labels are semantic categories like Health, Education, and Finance; others are relational lexicalized subtypes like Husband/BF and Wife/GF; and others are composite forms like Age/Gender. It is not obvious why some distinctions are split while others are merged. For example, Relationship Status, Husband/BF, and Wife/GF seem overlapping and potentially confusable, which is reflected in weaker per-class performance for some categories. The rule that disclosures about others should be labeled as Family rather than more specific categories also introduces asymmetry that may simplify annotation but weakens conceptual consistency. I would have liked a clearer justification for the taxonomy design, perhaps including alternatives considered, confusion patterns, and whether categories were chosen for privacy salience, frequency, annotatability, or downstream abstraction utility.

The identification modeling is straightforward and mostly sensible, but the experimental setup leaves several questions unanswered. Fine-tuning RoBERTa-large for sequence tagging is a reasonable baseline, and the sentence-level segmentation result is useful. However, the paper does not compare against stronger or more task-appropriate baselines beyond different chunking strategies. Since this is essentially a span extraction / NER-style task, comparisons to CRF heads, span-based models, instruction-tuned LLM tagging, or even simpler lexical/PII baselines would help contextualize the gains. The hybrid handling of rare classes via LUKE, Presidio, regexes, and a sentence classifier is practical, but it also makes the system definition somewhat fragmented. It is not fully clear how these components are integrated into the reported results: are the F1 scores in Table 2 for the RoBERTa tagger only, or for the full pipeline including external detectors? If the latter, how are overlaps/conflicts resolved? If the former, then the practical system performance on rare but high-risk classes is not actually quantified in the main results.

The evaluation metrics for identification are reasonable, especially the inclusion of exact span and partial span F1. Still, the reporting could be stronger. The paper reports averages over classes excluding O, but does not provide macro vs micro distinctions clearly, confidence intervals, or variance across runs. Given the modest dataset size and class imbalance, these details matter. Table 3 is informative and shows substantial heterogeneity across classes, with Sexual Orientation and Relationship Status notably weak at span level. This is important because some of the most privacy-sensitive categories are among the hardest. The paper should discuss this more directly rather than emphasizing the overall token F1 above 75, which somewhat overstates practical readiness. Token F1 is the most forgiving metric here; exact span F1 around 49 for multi-class and 54 for binary is much more indicative of user-facing utility.

The user study is a welcome addition and one of the more distinctive parts of the paper, but it should be interpreted carefully. The qualitative findings are interesting: users appreciate the concept, but want personalization, subreddit awareness, and explanations. These are valuable insights. However, the quantitative framing around “82% positive outlook” feels somewhat overstated given the small sample size of 21 participants, the formative nature of the study, and the fact that outputs were manually prepared for presentation. The study seems more like an exploratory interview study than a validation of real-world applicability in a strong empirical sense. Also, because participants supplied posts they already considered privacy-sensitive, there may be selection effects that make the tool appear more useful than it would in broader deployment. I would encourage the authors to present this component more explicitly as formative design research rather than as evidence that the model is deployment-ready.

The abstraction task is novel and potentially impactful, but this section is also the most methodologically fragile. The biggest concern is that both training and much of evaluation data are generated by LLMs. ChatGPT is used to generate train/eval abstractions and GPT-4 to generate test references. Then Llama 2 is fine-tuned to imitate these abstractions. This creates a synthetic teacher-student setup where the target behavior is largely defined by proprietary LLM outputs rather than human-authored gold standards. That is not necessarily invalid, but it substantially changes what is being measured. BLEU/ROUGE against GPT-generated references mostly assess imitation of another model’s style, not necessarily privacy reduction quality or user usefulness. The paper partly acknowledges this by including human evaluation, but the synthetic nature of the task data should be foregrounded much more clearly.

I also have concerns about the abstraction evaluation protocol. BLEU and ROUGE are weak metrics for this task because many valid abstractions can differ lexically from references, and privacy reduction is not well captured by n-gram overlap. The matching-based extension for three outputs is sensible for diversity-aware evaluation, but still inherits the same limitations. The human evaluation is therefore crucial, yet it appears limited. One author conducted the evaluation on 60 sampled instances, which raises concerns about bias and reliability. There is no report of multiple raters, inter-rater agreement, or blinding procedures. Since privacy reduction and utility preservation are subjective and central to the paper’s claims, single-annotator evaluation is not sufficient for strong conclusions. Moreover, the reported privacy reduction score of 3.19/5 is only moderate, which the paper states, but the broader narrative sometimes sounds more definitive than warranted. The coherence score of 93.7% is encouraging, but again would be more convincing with independent raters.

Another conceptual issue with abstraction is the threat model. The paper frames abstraction as reducing privacy risk while preserving utility, but privacy risk is not operationalized beyond human judgments of “detail removal.” In practice, privacy risk depends on adversarial inference, linkage attacks, and contextual uniqueness. Replacing “32” with “early 30s” may reduce specificity, but perhaps not meaningfully in some contexts; replacing “UCLA” with “a university” may help more. A stronger paper would either define a clearer privacy objective or include an auxiliary evaluation using attribute inference or re-identification risk before and after abstraction. Without such analysis, “privacy reduction” remains a subjective proxy. This is acceptable for an initial paper, but then claims should be correspondingly modest.

The paper’s ethical stance is thoughtful in some respects, especially around annotator protection and restricted release. However, one statement in the ethics section is too strong: “In cases where the models fail, they do not pose additional risks but rather tend towards overprotection.” I do not think this is justified. False negatives could absolutely pose additional risks if users overtrust the tool and fail to notice unflagged disclosures. Likewise, generated abstractions could introduce misleading or semantically altered content, or create a false sense of safety. The paper should discuss automation bias and under-warning as real risks. I also found the claim that no harms would disproportionately impact marginalized populations difficult to support, especially since the introduction itself notes that privacy risks are particularly acute for marginalized groups. Misclassification or inappropriate abstraction of identity-related disclosures could plausibly have uneven impacts.

There are also several presentation and clarity issues. The paper contains many grammatical errors and typos, including “broad the scope,” “fine-graiend,” “perform better,” “the loss are ignored,” and others. Some methodological descriptions are hard to parse, especially in the abstraction section. The tables are informative, but some captions and references are inconsistent, and the human evaluation columns in Table 5 are not fully self-explanatory in text. The paper would benefit from careful proofreading and tighter exposition.

Despite these concerns, I do think the paper has meaningful merit. The problem is important, the dataset appears useful, the span-level framing is practically motivated, and the user study surfaces real design tensions that purely benchmark-driven work would miss. The abstraction task, while preliminary, is creative and likely to inspire follow-up work. My main recommendation is not to reduce ambition, but to sharpen the empirical claims and strengthen the evidence around annotation quality and human evaluation.

For improvement, I would strongly encourage the authors to add inter-annotator agreement statistics for both post-level filtering and span/category annotation, along with clearer details on adjudication and annotation coverage. For identification, the paper should clarify whether the reported results are for the pure RoBERTa tagger or the full hybrid system, and ideally include stronger baselines and error analysis, especially for sensitive low-resource classes. For the user study, the authors should frame it as formative and avoid overgeneralizing from 21 participants. For abstraction, the most important improvements would be multi-rater human evaluation, clearer disclosure of the synthetic-reference setup, and if possible an additional privacy-oriented evaluation such as attribute inference reduction or uniqueness reduction before/after abstraction. Finally, the ethics discussion should acknowledge false negatives, overreliance, and differential harms more explicitly.

In summary, this is a thoughtful and original paper on a socially important problem. Its main strengths are the practical span-level framing, the new taxonomy/corpus, and the integration of user-centered inquiry with NLP modeling. Its main weaknesses are insufficient annotation reliability reporting, somewhat limited modeling baselines, and especially the preliminary nature of the abstraction evaluation, which relies heavily on LLM-generated references and limited human assessment. I view the work as a promising first step rather than a fully mature solution. If accepted, it would likely stimulate useful discussion and follow-up research, but I would want the final version to substantially tighten its methodological reporting and moderate some of its claims.

prompt_structured_json.summary: The paper addresses privacy risks in online self-disclosure by proposing two tasks: span-level self-disclosure identification and self-disclosure abstraction. It introduces a 19-category taxonomy, a Reddit-based corpus with 2.4K posts and 4.8K annotated disclosure spans, and fine-tunes RoBERTa-large for token tagging, reporting over 75 token-level F1 and around 49/54 span-level F1 for multi/binary settings. It also presents a formative user study with 21 Reddit users suggesting practical interest in such a tool. Motivated by this feedback, the paper proposes a new generation task that rewrites disclosure spans into less specific alternatives, training Llama-2-7B with LoRA on LLM-generated abstractions and evaluating with automatic metrics and limited human judgments, reporting moderate privacy reduction and high utility/diversity.
strengths: The paper tackles an important and underexplored problem: user-side privacy protection for voluntary self-disclosures rather than only classic PII redaction or attribute inference.
The span-level formulation is practically meaningful and more actionable than prior sentence/post-level disclosure classification.
The 19-category taxonomy is relatively broad and the annotation effort appears substantial, with in-house annotators, training, and adjudicated test data.
The identification experiments are reasonably thorough in comparing segmentation strategies and binary vs multi-class formulations.
The inclusion of an HCI-oriented user study is valuable and helps ground the task in realistic user needs.
The abstraction task is novel and potentially impactful, especially the idea of offering multiple diverse rewrites rather than a single redaction.
The paper is generally well motivated and connects NLP modeling with privacy and usability considerations.
weaknesses: The empirical support for the abstraction task is weak because training and much of evaluation data are generated by proprietary LLMs rather than humans, making it unclear whether the model learns genuine privacy-preserving abstraction or merely imitates GPT-style rewrites.
The abstraction dataset is very small (159/25/50 posts for train/dev/test from the most recent 10% subset), which raises concerns about robustness and generalization.

The human evaluation for abstraction is limited: only 60 sampled instances, apparently evaluated by one author in at least one stage, which introduces substantial bias and weakens claims of effectiveness.

The user study sample is small (21 participants), restricted to U.S. adult Reddit users, and the reported positive perception percentages should not be overinterpreted as evidence of broad real-world applicability.

The identification results are only moderate at exact span level (~49 multi, ~54 binary), with very poor performance on some sensitive classes such as sexual orientation and relationship status, limiting practical reliability.
The paper does not compare against strong modern baselines for sequence labeling or prompting-based extraction, nor against simpler privacy tools beyond descriptive discussion.
The decision not to release the dataset/models substantially limits reproducibility and scientific value.
The paper sometimes overstates conclusions, e.g., claiming real-world applicability and privacy protection despite limited external validation and modest exact-span performance.
methodological_flaws: Selection bias in corpus construction: only posts where two annotators initially agreed that personal disclosure exists were retained for span annotation. This may exclude ambiguous or subtle disclosures and inflate downstream performance by simplifying the task distribution.

The annotation protocol asks annotators to include contextual self-referential wording in spans (e.g., 'I live in the US' instead of 'US'), which conflates disclosure detection with span boundary conventions. Reported span metrics may therefore reflect annotation style as much as semantic detection ability.

For rare classes (name/contact), the system is a pipeline combining external tools and a sentence classifier, but these classes are excluded from the main multi-class results table. This makes the overall system performance across all 19 categories unclear and weakens the claim of broad-coverage modeling.

The abstraction training/evaluation setup has contamination risk in scientific logic: train/dev references are generated by ChatGPT while test references are generated by GPT-4, and the best model is described as 'distilled on GPT-4 generated abstractions' in the abstract. The exact provenance is confusing, and using LLM-generated references as ground truth undermines validity of lexical-overlap metrics and may bias human judgments toward LLM style.

Automatic metrics for abstraction (BLEU/ROUGE) are poorly aligned with the stated goals of privacy reduction and utility preservation. High overlap with references does not establish privacy protection, and no formal privacy-risk metric or adversarial re-identification evaluation is provided.

Human evaluation methodology is insufficiently rigorous: one stage is explicitly conducted by one of the authors, inter-rater agreement is not reported, and the number/independence of annotators for the final Likert evaluation is unclear. This is a serious empirical validity issue for the main abstraction claims.

The paper claims failures 'do not pose additional risks' and tend toward overprotection, but this is not scientifically justified. Under-detection of disclosures or misleading abstractions could plausibly increase risk, so the ethics statement overreaches.
No statistical significance testing or confidence intervals are reported for key comparisons in either identification or abstraction, despite many small differences being used to select best methods.
